title: Each link
hook: each generation passes the tradition to the next

segments.voice: Yesterday, zachor, and your line: a memory that leads to doing. Did you write down one memory before it slipped away? This is the week's last day: food, music, repair, the synagogue, a candle, a memory. Today, how all of it gets from one pair of hands to the next. Day one thousand fifty-seven.

Moses received the Torah from Sinai, and handed it on to Joshua. That is how Pirkei Avot begins, the part of the Mishnah whose name means the Chapters of the Fathers. It does not open with a law, or a blessing, or a wise saying. It opens with a relay. Joshua hands it to the elders. The elders hand it to the prophets. The prophets hand it to the men of the Great Assembly. Nobody in that sentence invents anything. Every person in it does exactly two things: receives, and passes on. Today's word is the place each of them stands.
screen: `MOSES RECEIVED IT, AND HANDED IT ON.` → `NOT A LAW: A RELAY.` → `RECEIVE, AND PASS ON.`

segments.voice: Each link. Tradition calls this line of hands shalshelet ha-kabbalah, the chain of tradition. Look at its two verbs. In Hebrew, Moses kibel, received, and masar, handed over. Received is a humble word. The Torah came to Moses; it didn't start with him. Handed over is a trusting word. It means letting go of something precious and putting it into someone else's hands. Then the Great Assembly speaks, and one of its three sayings is this: raise up many disciples. So the chain was never meant to be a single thread. Each link is told to reach toward many next links. The Torah itself puts the chain somewhere smaller than a school. In the Shema, Deuteronomy says, "and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children", and then it names the places: sitting in your house, walking by the way, lying down, rising up. A kitchen counts. A car ride counts. Look back over this week and the same chain shows up in other forms. A recipe handed down. A melody. A candle lit on the right date. A memory written down so it won't vanish. None of it lasts by being admired. It lasts by being handed over. And a chain has one more thing to teach. Nobody holds the whole of it. Each link touches the one before it and reaches toward the ones after, and that small reach is the whole job. That's today's line: each link.
screen: `RECEIVED, AND HANDED OVER.` · `RAISE UP MANY DISCIPLES.` · `TEACH THEM UNTO THY CHILDREN.` · `A RECIPE, A MELODY, A CANDLE.` · then, large: `EACH LINK.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: tell one family story. Settle, and let your breath slow. Bring up one story from your family: how two people met, how someone arrived in a new place, a meal, a mistake everyone still laughs about. It doesn't need to be important. Find the version you heard, the way it was told to you. Then tell it once in your head, slowly, with the details left in: the weather, the clothes, the exact words someone said. Notice which detail you would never want dropped. If you pray, you can give thanks for the person who handed it to you. If you don't, just hold their name for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Each link. One place in the chain of tradition: a person who receives and hands on, touching the one before and the one after. Today's word.
Your line: receives, and passes on. Today, tell one family story out loud to someone who hasn't heard it, and say who told it to you first. Day one thousand fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Pirkei Avot, which opens with the chain from Moses onward, is studied in synagogues and at home, and families pass the tradition on at home: at the Shabbat table, at the Passover Seder, and in stories told to children and grandchildren.

fork.setup: you're one of the men of the Great Assembly. the Torah has been handed to you through Moses, Joshua, the elders and the prophets. what do you tell the next generation?
options: guard it closely, and teach only a chosen few.
write it all down, and stop teaching.
fork.reveal: raise up many disciples, one of the Great Assembly's three sayings. the chain was meant to branch, not stay a single thread.

original.note: Hebrew: handed over, the verb Pirkei Avot uses for Moses passing the Torah to Joshua.

trapdoor: what you thought: the chain of tradition is a line of famous rabbis.
what it means: everyone who receives the tradition and hands it on, at a kitchen table as much as in a school.
what a scholar hears: Avot 1:1's two verbs, kibel and masar, received and handed over, and a Great Assembly whose answer is raise up many disciples.
